topic: What Is State Management & Why It Matters

questions.question: What is state management in React and how do you choose an approach?
questions.title: What Is State Management
questions.direct_answer: State management is organizing where state lives and how components access it. The spectrum: component state (useState — local, first choice), lifted state (shared with siblings via a common ancestor), Context (subtree-wide for low-frequency data like theme/auth), URL state (filters, tabs — shareable and survives refresh), server cache (React Query/SWR — server data with caching, NOT client state), and external stores (Zustand/Redux — global, selector-based re-renders for high-frequency or cross-page state). Choose the simplest level that fits; add complexity only when measured pain demands it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: State management is organizing where state lives and how components access it. The spectrum: component state (useState — local, first choice), lifted state (shared with siblings via a common ancestor), Context (subtree-wide for low-frequency data like theme/auth), URL state (filters, tabs — shareable and survives refresh), server cache (React Query/SWR — server data with caching, NOT client state), and external stores (Zustand/Redux — global, selector-based re-renders for high-frequency or cross-page state). Choose the simplest level that fits; add complexity only when measured pain demands it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The decision ladder (the interview answer):

```
1. LOCAL (useState/useReducer) — default. 95% of state.
2. LIFTED — when siblings need it. The React-native sharing mechanism.
3. URL (searchParams/router state) — when it's navigation-shaped:
   filters, tabs, pagination. Shareable links + refresh-survives free.
4. SERVER CACHE (React Query/SWR) — server data is NOT your state:
   it's a cache. The library owns fetching/loading/invalidation.
5. CONTEXT — global + low-frequency: theme, auth user, locale.
6. STORE (Zustand/Redux) — global + high-frequency, or cross-page,
   or needs devtools/middleware/persistence.
```

The classification skill (what separates candidates): before choosing a tool, classify the STATE KIND:
- Server data (users, orders, prices) → server-cache library. Copying it into Redux and syncing manually is the classic anti-pattern — stale lists, loading spinners reinvented, cache invalidation bugs.
- Client UI state (modals open, form inputs, hover) → local. Almost never global.
- Client app state (auth, cart, selected theme) → context or store by frequency.
- URL-shaped state (active tab, search, page) → URL. If refreshing should preserve it or a link should reproduce it, it's URL state.

The store comparison in one line each (the follow-up you'll get): Zustand — tiny, hook-based, selector subscriptions, no Provider wrapper; Redux Toolkit — mature devtools/middleware/pattern, more structure, good for large teams' conventions; Context — zero deps, built-in, but broadcasts re-renders. Jotai/Recoil — atomic state, fine-grained. MobX — observable/reactive model.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[state to place] --> K{what KIND?}
    K -->|server data| Q[server cache: React Query / SWR]
    K -->|one component| L[useState local]
    K -->|siblings share| LF[lift to common ancestor]
    K -->|navigation-shaped| U[URL: searchParams]
    K -->|global, low freq| C[Context]
    K -->|global, high freq / cross-page| Z[store: Zustand / Redux + selectors]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the default must stay local (the architecture reasoning): global state couples every component that touches it to a shared contract — refactors ripple, tests need the store, re-render scope grows. Local state keeps components independently testable and removable. The teams that put everything in a store 'for consistency' recreate the problems state libraries were invented to solve (coupling), just with extra tooling — the anti-pattern Redux's own docs now warn against.

The server-cache insight (the modern shift): ~80% of what apps called 'state' was fetched server data being stored client-side. React Query/SWR reframed it: that's a CACHE (stale-while-revalidate, background refetch, invalidation by query key, deduping concurrent requests for the same key). Moving it out of the store shrinks the client store to genuinely client data (auth, cart, UI), which is usually small enough that Context or a tiny store suffices — many apps deleted Redux entirely after this reclassification.

The re-render economics (the selection criterion that matters): every mechanism differs in WHO re-renders on a change. useState: the component (+ default subtree). Context: every consumer of that context (memo can't stop it). Zustand/Redux with selectors: only components reading the changed slice (verified shape: a selector on count doesn't fire when user changes — the subscription compares the selected value). This single property — subscription granularity — is the technical answer to 'why not just context for everything?'
